newsitem.title: USA: US venture capital group wants more lawsuit reform.
newsitem.headline: US venture capital group wants more lawsuit reform.

text.p: A group of 700 entrepeneurs and venture capitalists on Tuesday urged Congress to help stop securities class actions suits from migrating to state courts.
The group pressed House and Senate leaders to move quickly on legislation introduced last month in the House that aims to curb what these firms called frivolous lawsuits.

"Meaningful national securities litigation reform which cannot be circumvented by state laws is an absolutely critical issue to emgerging growth companies and those who invest in them," the group wrote in a letter to several lawmakers including House and Senate Republican leaders.
Although the group won restrictions in 1995 over a presidential veto affecting federal law, many of these lawsuits are now headed for state courts, the group said.

"For years the very companies that are creating the largest share of this Nation's jobs in some of the most far reaching technological and medical fields have been victimized by abusive securities suits," the group wrote.

But consumer groups, state representatives and trial lawyers, who fought the 1995 litigation reforms, warn that investors cannot be stripped of more legal rights. And the prospects of imposing new reforms have received a lukewarm response from President Clinton and Securities and Exchange Commission chairman Arthur Levitt.

"We think this legislation is a terrible idea for investors. We have very little experience under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995," Jeffrey Klafter, a partner with the New York law firm Bernstein Litowitz Berger and Grossmann, told Reuters. He said that, under federal law, investors are faced with a one year statute of limitations, leaving state courts as often the only alternative.

"We can't wait for government organizations to spend their years doing investigations," he said. "There are major major frauds that do not come to light until more than three years after the time of the investment. Investors would simply be out of court unless they could pursue state law remedies."
